DefaultTab.Hint: Which tab is active when the window opens.

ReplaceOnlySheet.Name: Only-Sheet: show button
ReplaceOnlySheet.Hint: Injects an NDRS button into the Only-Sheet button bar.

Attack.Title: Attack
Attack.Subtitle: A melee or ranged attack against a target in reach.
Attack.Summary: The Attack action lets you make one attack roll against a target's Armor Class. If you have the Extra Attack class feature you can make multiple attacks within the same action. The Unarmed Strike option folds Damage, Grapple and Shove into the Attack action — Grapple and Shove replace the damage with an effect. A weapon may use one of its mastery property options per Attack action, provided you are proficient with it.
Attack.Example: A level-5 Fighter takes two attacks (Extra Attack), and chooses on the second swing to Shove the target prone with an Unarmed Strike instead of dealing damage.
Attack.Notes: 2024 unifies Grapple, Shove, and a basic punch as options of the Unarmed Strike — none of them are separate actions any longer.

Magic.Title: Magic
Magic.Subtitle: Activate a magic item or trigger an item's spell-effect that requires an action.
Magic.Summary: The Magic action covers the use of magic items whose activation requires an action — wands, scrolls, potions, and item features that explicitly call for a Magic action. It does not replace casting one of your own spells; that uses the dedicated spellcasting actions and timing rules.
Magic.Example: A Rogue draws a scroll of Identify and uses the Magic action to discharge its effect on a ring the party recovered from the vault.

Dash.Title: Dash
Dash.Subtitle: Gain extra movement equal to your current speed.
Dash.Summary: Dash effectively doubles your movement for the turn: you gain extra distance equal to your current speed (after all modifiers like difficult terrain or exhaustion). The extra movement may be used in any order, including split before and after other actions you take this turn.
Dash.Example: A Monk with 40 ft of speed takes Dash and can cover up to 80 ft this turn — perfect for sprinting out of an archer's line of sight into cover.

Disengage.Title: Disengage
Disengage.Subtitle: Your movement until the end of the turn does not provoke opportunity attacks.
Disengage.Summary: Disengage prevents your movement from triggering opportunity attacks until the end of your turn, in exchange for your action. Reach itself is not magically ignored — only the Opportunity Attack reaction is suppressed by this action.
Disengage.Example: A Wizard ended his last turn engaged with an Orc. Rather than risk the trip back, he Disengages and safely walks 30 ft away to cast at range.

Dodge.Title: Dodge
Dodge.Subtitle: Attacks against you have disadvantage; your Dexterity saves have advantage.
Dodge.Summary: Until the start of your next turn, attacks against you have disadvantage as long as you can see the attacker and you are not incapacitated. You also roll Dexterity saving throws with advantage. The benefit ends if your speed drops to 0 or you become incapacitated.
Dodge.Example: A wounded Cleric facing two Goblins skips attacking and Dodges instead — both Goblins must roll their attacks against him with disadvantage this round.

Subtitle.metric: Grant an ally advantage on a roll — attack target must be within 1.5 m.
Subtitle.imperial: Grant an ally advantage on a roll — attack target must be within 5 ft.

Summary.metric: Help has two clearly separated forms: (1) you assist an ally's ability check on a task you can meaningfully contribute to — the ally rolls with advantage. (2) You distract an enemy within 1.5 m of you; the next attack roll an ally makes against that enemy before the start of your next turn has advantage.
Summary.imperial: Help has two clearly separated forms: (1) you assist an ally's ability check on a task you can meaningfully contribute to — the ally rolls with advantage. (2) You distract an enemy within 5 ft of you; the next attack roll an ally makes against that enemy before the start of your next turn has advantage.

Example.metric: The Rogue stands adjacent to an Ogre guard. She Helps the Fighter: the Fighter's next attack against the Ogre has advantage.
Example.imperial: The Rogue stands adjacent to an Ogre guard. She Helps the Fighter: the Fighter's next attack against the Ogre has advantage.

Notes.metric: New in 2024: Helping with an ability check now requires that you can meaningfully contribute to the task — pure cheering does not qualify.
Notes.imperial: New in 2024: Helping with an ability check now requires that you can meaningfully contribute to the task — pure cheering does not qualify.

Hide.Title: Hide
Hide.Subtitle: Stealth check vs DC 15; on success you gain the Invisible condition.
Hide.Summary: You make a Dexterity (Stealth) check with DC 15 while you have cover or are heavily obscured. On success you gain the Invisible condition. The condition ends as soon as you make a noise louder than a whisper, attack, cast a spell with a verbal component, or are seen — for example by leaving cover.
Hide.Example: The Ranger ducks behind a wagon, rolls a 18 on Stealth, and gains the Invisible condition. The next attack from cover has advantage — but that attack also ends the hidden state.
Hide.Notes: New in 2024: Hide explicitly grants the Invisible condition and uses a fixed DC 15 instead of a passive-Perception contest.

Influence.Title: Influence
Influence.Subtitle: Get an NPC to do something via Persuasion, Deception, Intimidation, or Performance.
Influence.Summary: Influence is the formal action for social manipulation in play. You choose to persuade, deceive, intimidate, or perform, and roll the appropriate Charisma check against a DC tied to the NPC's attitude. A creature that does not understand your language, or one that is hostile, cannot be influenced — the action fails automatically.
Influence.Example: A Bard tries to talk a city guard captain into releasing a prisoner. The DM sets the DC at 15 because the captain is friendly — the Bard rolls Persuasion.
Influence.Notes: New in 2024: social interaction is now a defined action with a documented framework, rather than purely free-form roleplay.

Ready.Title: Ready
Ready.Subtitle: Set a trigger and execute an action or movement later as a reaction.
Ready.Summary: You describe a perceivable trigger ("when the Goblin steps through the door") and an action or movement to take in response. Until then your action is spent; the later execution consumes your reaction. If the trigger does not occur before the start of your next turn, the readied action is wasted. Readying a spell expends the slot at the moment of readying — the spell also requires concentration to hold.
Ready.Example: The Wizard says: "As soon as anyone opens the trapdoor, I cast Magic Missile." The DM narrates the Goblin opening it — the Wizard spends his reaction, the spell triggers.

Search.Title: Search
Search.Subtitle: A Wisdom check to find something concealed or a hidden creature.
Search.Summary: With Search you make a Wisdom check — typically Perception, Insight, or Survival — to look for tracks, a hidden creature, a concealed compartment, or to read a creature's body language. Against a creature that has hidden, the DC is its Stealth result (or DC 15 if the DM keeps that result hidden).
Search.Example: The Ranger investigates an abandoned watchtower, rolls 17 on Perception, and finds fresh footprints — the DM describes them as medium-size, less than an hour old.

Study.Title: Study
Study.Subtitle: An Intelligence check to recall lore or analyze a creature, object, or phenomenon.
Study.Summary: Study is the action you take to draw on your background knowledge or to analyze something in detail. Depending on the question you roll Arcana, History, Nature, Religion, or Investigation. On success you learn a relevant fact, a hint, or a vulnerability — the exact information is at the DM's discretion.
Study.Example: Facing a Gargoyle guardian, the Cleric rolls Religion via Study and recalls its weakness to bludgeoning damage — the DM grants a narrative hint.
Study.Notes: New in 2024: Study replaces the 2014-era mix of "Search" and "recall lore" — Intelligence-based checks are now an explicit action of their own.

Utilize.Title: Utilize
Utilize.Subtitle: Operate a non-magical object that requires an action to use.
Utilize.Summary: Utilize covers the use of mundane objects whose activation requires an action — pulling a lever, opening a lock with the right key, ringing a bell, or beating a drum, when those mechanically demand an action. Magic items use the Magic action; Utilize is the mundane counterpart.
Utilize.Example: The Dwarf Fighter stands before a rusty wall lever. He uses Utilize to throw it — the trapdoor under the troll's table swings open.

Overview.Title: Bonus Action
Overview.Subtitle: An additional, short action — only when a feature explicitly grants one.
Overview.Summary: Bonus actions are not a free slot — you can take one in a turn only when a class feature, spell, feat, or weapon mastery explicitly offers one. A turn allows exactly one bonus action regardless of how many sources you have. A bonus action does not consume your reaction or your action.
Overview.Example: A Rogue takes the Attack action and then uses Cunning Action as a bonus action to Hide — both stem from clearly defined class features.

OffHand.Title: Off-Hand Attack
OffHand.Subtitle: Attack with a Light weapon in your other hand if your main attack used a Light melee weapon.
OffHand.Summary: If you take the Attack action with a Light melee weapon, you may use a bonus action to make one additional attack with another Light weapon held in your free hand. Your ability modifier adds to the bonus-attack damage only if it is negative — otherwise only the weapon die counts.
OffHand.Example: A Rogue attacks with a Shortsword (Light property) and uses a bonus action to attack again with her Dagger — the bonus attack deals only weapon-die damage, no Dexterity modifier.
OffHand.Notes: New in 2024: Two-Weapon Fighting is now a universal weapon option keyed off the Light property, no longer a separate fighting style on its own.

Spell.Title: Bonus Action Spell
Spell.Subtitle: Spells whose casting time is a bonus action (e.g. Healing Word).
Spell.Summary: Some spells have a casting time of 1 bonus action. A central rule applies: when you cast a bonus-action spell during your turn, the only spell you may cast as your regular action that turn is a cantrip — no second leveled spell.
Spell.Example: The Cleric casts Healing Word as a bonus action on the falling Fighter, then in the same turn casts only a cantrip like Sacred Flame, never a second leveled spell.
Spell.Notes: The "one-spell-per-turn" rule is cleanly worded in 2024: the cantrip is allowed as the action, a second leveled spell is not.

Class.Title: Class Bonus Actions
Class.Subtitle: Class-specific bonus actions — see your class entry.
Class.Summary: Many class features grant their own bonus actions: a Monk's Flurry of Blows, a Rogue's Cunning Action, a Barbarian's Rage, a Paladin's Divine Smite, to name only a few. Check your class description for the trigger and any per-day or per-rest limit.
Class.Example: A Monk takes the Attack action and then uses Flurry of Blows as a bonus action to add two unarmed strikes via Ki points.

Overview.Title: Reaction
Overview.Subtitle: A once-per-round response to a trigger outside your turn.
Overview.Summary: You have exactly one reaction per round, refreshed at the start of your next turn. Reactions are triggered by clearly described events — you must perceive the trigger, and your response resolves immediately. Movement reactions do not interrupt the triggering creature's turn unless the description says otherwise.
Overview.Example: A Fighter sees a Goblin shaman casting a spell and uses her reaction for Counterspell — assuming she knows the spell herself.

Subtitle.metric: When a visible enemy leaves your reach, you make one melee attack.
Subtitle.imperial: When a visible enemy leaves your reach, you make one melee attack.

Summary.metric: When a creature you can see moves out of your reach, you may use your reaction to make one melee attack against it. The attack uses whatever weapon you currently wield (unarmed counts). Movement such as teleportation, the Disengage action, forced movement, or moving into your reach does not trigger an opportunity attack.
Summary.imperial: When a creature you can see moves out of your reach, you may use your reaction to make one melee attack against it. The attack uses whatever weapon you currently wield (unarmed counts). Movement such as teleportation, the Disengage action, forced movement, or moving into your reach does not trigger an opportunity attack.

Example.metric: A Goblin tries to run past the Fighter to reach the Wizard. The Fighter takes her reaction and swings her sword as soon as the Goblin leaves her reach.
Example.imperial: A Goblin tries to run past the Fighter to reach the Wizard. The Fighter takes her reaction and swings her sword as soon as the Goblin leaves her reach.

Notes.metric: The Disengage action prevents opportunity attacks for that turn. A creature you cannot see never triggers an opportunity attack.
Notes.imperial: The Disengage action prevents opportunity attacks for that turn. A creature you cannot see never triggers an opportunity attack.

Ready.Title: Readied Reaction
Ready.Subtitle: A previously readied action triggers now.
Ready.Summary: The reaction half of the Ready action. When the trigger you specified occurs, you spend your reaction and execute the planned action or movement. If the trigger does not occur before the start of your next turn, the readying is lost.
Ready.Example: The Archer has readied a draw aimed at the doorframe. As soon as the first Goblin slips through, the reaction triggers — the arrow flies.

Spell.Title: Reaction Spells
Spell.Subtitle: Spells with a casting time of 1 reaction — Shield, Feather Fall, Counterspell.
Spell.Summary: Some spells have a casting time of 1 reaction tied to a specific trigger described in the spell. They consume a slot (cantrips none) and your reaction this round. Remember: only one reaction per round — if you cast Shield as a reaction, you have no reaction left until the start of your next turn.
Spell.Example: The Wizard is hit by an arrow that would just barely beat her AC. She casts Shield as a reaction: +5 AC until the start of her next turn — the arrow misses.

Subtitle.metric: Your speed defines how far you can move in a single turn.
Subtitle.imperial: Your speed defines how far you can move in a single turn.

Summary.metric: On your turn you have movement points equal to your speed — the standard speed for most player characters is 9 m. You may freely interleave movement with action, bonus action, and free interactions. You can save part of your movement for later in the same turn, but anything unspent at turn end is lost.
Summary.imperial: On your turn you have movement points equal to your speed — the standard speed for most player characters is 30 ft. You may freely interleave movement with action, bonus action, and free interactions. You can save part of your movement for later in the same turn, but anything unspent at turn end is lost.

Example.metric: A Halfling Rogue with 7.5 m of speed moves 4.5 m forward, attacks a Goblin, then slips 3 m behind a column.
Example.imperial: A Halfling Rogue with 25 ft of speed moves 15 ft forward, attacks a Goblin, then slips 10 ft behind a column.

Difficult.Title: Difficult Terrain
Difficult.Subtitle: Each step in difficult terrain costs double movement.
Difficult.Summary: Swamp, dense rubble, low furniture, or thick undergrowth count as difficult terrain. Each foot of movement costs double. Difficult terrain does not stack with itself — double remains double, not quadruple. Specific effects can make steps even more expensive; their description will say so explicitly.
Difficult.Example: A Wizard with 30 ft speed wants to walk through a 20 ft rubble field. The 20 ft of difficult terrain cost 40 ft — she just barely makes it across with no movement to spare.

Subtitle.metric: Long jump = Strength score in feet (~0.30 m per point). High jump = 90 cm + 30 cm per Str mod.
Subtitle.imperial: Long jump = Strength score in feet. High jump = 3 + Str modifier in feet.

Summary.metric: With at least 3 m of running start, your long jump distance equals your Strength score in feet (so STR 16 ≈ 4.8 m). Your high jump reaches 90 cm plus 30 cm per Strength modifier. From a standstill both values are halved. Each foot of jumping consumes the equivalent foot of your movement.
Summary.imperial: With at least 10 ft of running start, your long jump distance equals your Strength score in feet (so STR 16 ≈ 16 ft). Your high jump reaches 3 ft plus 1 ft per Strength modifier. From a standstill both values are halved. Each foot of jumping consumes the equivalent foot of your movement.

Example.metric: A Barbarian with Strength 18 takes a 9 m running start and jumps 5.4 m across a chasm.
Example.imperial: A Barbarian with Strength 18 takes a 30 ft running start and jumps 18 ft across a chasm.

Notes.metric: Jump distance can never exceed your remaining movement — if you run out mid-air, you fall.
Notes.imperial: Jump distance can never exceed your remaining movement — if you run out mid-air, you fall.

Climb.Title: Climbing
Climb.Subtitle: Climbing costs double movement — or normal movement if you have a climb speed.
Climb.Summary: When climbing walls, trees, or ropes, each step costs double movement. With an innate climb speed (some species, certain forms) you pay the regular movement cost. Particularly slick or sheer surfaces may also call for a Strength (Athletics) check — the DM decides per situation.
Climb.Example: A Rogue climbs 15 ft up a building wall — costing 30 ft of his 30 ft of speed. He has nothing left to do this turn.

Swim.Title: Swimming
Swim.Subtitle: Swimming costs double movement — unless you have a swim speed.
Swim.Summary: Swimming works like climbing: double movement cost, regular cost with a swim speed. Strong currents or storms may additionally require a Strength (Athletics) check. Heavy armor or significant load affect swimming — the DM may forbid forward progress in extreme conditions.
Swim.Example: A Wizard in robes swims through a calm river: 15 ft of distance costs 30 ft of movement. Add a storm and an Athletics check is in order.

Crawl.Title: Crawling
Crawl.Subtitle: While prone, every step of movement costs double.
Crawl.Summary: While you have the Prone condition, each foot of movement costs double. You cannot vault obstacles you would otherwise step around, and low ceilings often force you to crawl. Standing up from prone costs half your speed (see the "Stand Up" card).
Crawl.Example: A Cleric is on the ground but wants to crawl closer to the falling Fighter. Crawling 5 ft costs 10 ft of her 30 ft of speed.

Subtitle.metric: 1d6 bludgeoning damage per 3 m fallen, capped at 20d6.
Subtitle.imperial: 1d6 bludgeoning damage per 10 ft fallen, capped at 20d6.

Summary.metric: Without a soft landing you take 1d6 bludgeoning damage per 3 m of falling distance. The cap sits at 20d6 — about 60 m of fall reaches the mechanical maximum. You land Prone unless a magical effect like Feather Fall intervenes.
Summary.imperial: Without a soft landing you take 1d6 bludgeoning damage per 10 ft of falling distance. The cap sits at 20d6 — about 200 ft of fall reaches the mechanical maximum. You land Prone unless a magical effect like Feather Fall intervenes.

Example.metric: A Rogue falls 9 m and takes 3d6 bludgeoning damage — landing prone.
Example.imperial: A Rogue falls 30 ft and takes 3d6 bludgeoning damage — landing prone.

Notes.metric: Soft surfaces (hay, water) can reduce or negate damage at the DM's narration.
Notes.imperial: Soft surfaces (hay, water) can reduce or negate damage at the DM's narration.

StandUp.Title: Stand Up
StandUp.Subtitle: Standing up from prone costs half your speed.
StandUp.Summary: While Prone, standing up costs half your speed (rounded by DM ruling). If your remaining movement is too low, you cannot stand up this turn. Some features let you stand up at no cost or as a bonus action — check your class or feat descriptions.
StandUp.Example: A Fighter with 30 ft speed stands up from prone (15 ft consumed) and uses the remaining 15 ft to close on the Goblin.

Blinded.Title: Blinded
Blinded.Subtitle: You cannot see — attacks against you have advantage, your attacks have disadvantage.
Blinded.Summary: Sight is impossible; any check that requires sight automatically fails. Attack rolls against you have advantage, your own have disadvantage. Effects that require sight (like Opportunity Attacks against movement, some spells) do not function.
Blinded.Example: A Wizard is blinded by a Dust Devil. Until he frees himself, he misses the Storm Giant twice with disadvantage, while the giant lands its swing easily with advantage.
Blinded.Notes: Magical sight like Truesight or Tremorsense can bypass or compensate for Blinded depending on its description.

Charmed.Title: Charmed
Charmed.Subtitle: You cannot attack the charmer; they have advantage on social checks against you.
Charmed.Summary: You cannot attack the creature that charmed you, nor target it directly with a harmful effect. The charming creature also has advantage on Charisma checks aimed at influencing you. You remain otherwise capable — allies of the charmer are still fair game.
Charmed.Example: A Dryad casts Charm Person on the Fighter. The Fighter cannot attack the Dryad, but her Goblin guards are still valid targets.
Charmed.Notes: Charmed does not turn a creature into a puppet — it only protects the charmer from direct aggression.

Deafened.Title: Deafened
Deafened.Subtitle: You cannot hear — auditory checks fail automatically.
Deafened.Summary: Hearing is impossible; any check that requires hearing automatically fails. You can still cast spells with verbal components if you can speak — you just do not hear the result. Warnings or commands meant to alert you do not reach you.
Deafened.Example: A Bard is deafened by a Thunderclap. He cannot hear the approaching Rogues, losing the edge their loud footsteps would have given him.
Deafened.Notes: Telepathic communication is unaffected by Deafened — it bypasses hearing entirely.

Frightened.Title: Frightened
Frightened.Subtitle: You roll with disadvantage while you can see the source, and cannot willingly approach it.
Frightened.Summary: While you can see the source of your fear, ability checks and attack rolls have disadvantage. You cannot willingly move closer to the source. Breaking line of sight removes the disadvantage but the condition itself remains — you keep fleeing.
Frightened.Example: A Dragon uses its Frightful Presence. The Fighter fails the saving throw — frightened, he backs away and attacks the next round only with disadvantage.
Frightened.Notes: Effects like Bless against fear or magical resistance to fear can suppress the condition entirely.

Grappled.Title: Grappled
Grappled.Subtitle: Your speed becomes 0; attacks against creatures other than the grappler have disadvantage.
Grappled.Summary: Your speed drops to 0 and bonuses to speed do not apply. Your attack rolls against any creature other than the grappler have disadvantage. The condition ends when you escape (Strength or Dexterity check vs the grapple DC) or when the grappler becomes incapacitated.
Grappled.Example: A Giant Crab grabs the Fighter with its claw. The Fighter is grappled, cannot move, and can only meaningfully attack the crab itself.
Grappled.Notes: New in 2024: Grappling is now an option of the Attack action (Unarmed Strike → Grapple). The DC is 8 + Strength mod + proficiency of the grappler.

Incapacitated.Title: Incapacitated
Incapacitated.Subtitle: No actions, no bonus actions, no reactions. You also lose concentration on spells.
Incapacitated.Summary: While incapacitated you cannot take an action or bonus action on your turn, and no reaction outside your turn. Concentration on a spell breaks. Movement is not directly blocked — that comes from a paired condition like Prone, Grappled, or Unconscious.
Incapacitated.Example: A Wizard is hit by Hold Person — paralyzed and therefore also incapacitated. His concentration spell Bless on the party drops immediately.
Incapacitated.Notes: New in 2024: Incapacitated is cleanly described as the shared building block of many other conditions — it sits inside Paralyzed, Unconscious, Petrified, Stunned.

Invisible.Title: Invisible
Invisible.Subtitle: Others cannot see you; attacks have advantage/disadvantage in your favor.
Invisible.Summary: You cannot be seen — creatures relying on sight cannot directly target you. As long as you remain undetected, you have advantage on attacks against visible targets, and attacks against you have disadvantage. Sound, smell, or physical traces can give you away — the DM decides when.
Invisible.Example: A Monk drinks a potion of invisibility, sneaks up on a cultist, and attacks with advantage — the first strike reveals her position.
Invisible.Notes: New in 2024: the Hide action explicitly grants this condition — not just "hidden".

Paralyzed.Title: Paralyzed
Paralyzed.Subtitle: Incapacitated + immobile. Hits within reach are automatic critical hits.
Paralyzed.Summary: You are incapacitated and cannot move or speak. Strength and Dexterity saving throws fail automatically. Attacks against you have advantage, and any hit within 1.5 m / 5 ft is automatically a critical hit.
Paralyzed.Example: A Deep Wizard is paralyzed by a spell. The enemy Fighter swings in melee — every hit is automatically critical.
Paralyzed.Notes: Concentration spells break automatically (consequence of Incapacitated).

Petrified.Title: Petrified
Petrified.Subtitle: Turned to stone. Heavy resistances, but Strength/Dex saves fail automatically.
Petrified.Summary: Your body becomes stone. You are incapacitated, immobile, and unaware. You do not age. You gain resistance to all damage and immunity to poison and many diseases — but you are trivially easy to hit because Strength and Dexterity saves fail automatically.
Petrified.Example: A Wizard is hit by a Basilisk's gaze, fails the saving throw, and is petrified. Until a healing spell intervenes, he is out of the fight.
Petrified.Notes: Petrification is usually not undone by ordinary healing — Greater Restoration or Stone to Flesh is needed.

Poisoned.Title: Poisoned
Poisoned.Subtitle: Attack rolls and ability checks have disadvantage.
Poisoned.Summary: You roll attack rolls and ability checks with disadvantage. Saving throws are not affected. Source and duration depend on the trigger — some poisons last one round, others until the next day, some can be ended early by a saving throw.
Poisoned.Example: A Rogue is bitten by a spider — she fails the first saving throw and is poisoned for an hour, with disadvantage on every attack.
Poisoned.Notes: Resistance to poison damage is not the same as immunity to the Poisoned condition — these are often confused.

Prone.Title: Prone
Prone.Subtitle: You crawl. Melee attacks against you have advantage; ranged attacks have disadvantage.
Prone.Summary: While prone, every foot of movement costs double (crawling). Standing up costs half your speed. Melee attacks against you have advantage, ranged attacks against you have disadvantage. Your own attacks have disadvantage — melee or ranged.
Prone.Example: A Fighter is shoved prone. He stays prone until his next turn — the Goblins in melee attack with advantage, the Archer further back with disadvantage.
Prone.Notes: Unconscious and Petrified include Prone as well.

Restrained.Title: Restrained
Restrained.Subtitle: Speed 0, attacks against you with advantage, Dexterity saves with disadvantage.
Restrained.Summary: Your speed becomes 0. Attack rolls against you have advantage and your own have disadvantage. Dexterity saving throws are also at disadvantage. The condition is usually maintained by a source — webbing, vines, magical effects — and ends when you escape or the source is removed.
Restrained.Example: A Rogue is restrained by an Entangle spell. He cannot reach the Goblin archer, rolls his Dex saves with disadvantage, and is easy prey in melee.
Restrained.Notes: Restrained differs from Grappled: only Restrained imposes disadvantage on attacks targeting you and on your Dex saves.

Stunned.Title: Stunned
Stunned.Subtitle: Incapacitated, speed 0, Strength/Dex saves fail automatically.
Stunned.Summary: You are incapacitated, cannot move, and speak only haltingly. Strength and Dexterity saving throws fail automatically. Attacks against you have advantage.
Stunned.Example: A Monk uses Stunning Strike; the Goblin fails the save and is stunned — the Rogue immediately uses the advantage for Sneak Attack.
Stunned.Notes: Concentration on a spell breaks (consequence of Incapacitated).

Unconscious.Title: Unconscious
Unconscious.Subtitle: Incapacitated, prone, dropping items, Strength/Dex saves fail automatically.
Unconscious.Summary: You lose consciousness, are unaware of your surroundings, and fall — you gain the Prone condition as part of being unconscious. You drop whatever you were holding. Strength and Dexterity saving throws fail automatically. Attacks against you have advantage; melee hits within 1.5 m / 5 ft are automatic critical hits.
Unconscious.Example: A Fighter drops to 0 HP and falls unconscious. He lies on the ground, drops his sword, and must roll death saving throws.
Unconscious.Notes: New in 2024: Unconscious now explicitly includes the Prone condition — there is no longer a separate mention of "prone" needed.

Exhaustion.Title: Exhaustion (2024)
Exhaustion.Intro: Exhaustion has 6 cumulative levels. Each level adds −2 to all d20 tests (attacks, saves, ability checks) and reduces speed by 5 ft (1.5 m). Level 6 means death.
Exhaustion.L1: −2 on all d20 tests · −5 ft / −1.5 m speed
Exhaustion.L2: −4 on all d20 tests · −10 ft / −3.0 m speed
Exhaustion.L3: −6 on all d20 tests · −15 ft / −4.5 m speed
Exhaustion.L4: −8 on all d20 tests · −20 ft / −6.0 m speed
Exhaustion.L5: −10 on all d20 tests · −25 ft / −7.5 m speed
Exhaustion.Notes: A long rest reduces exhaustion by one level (assuming you eat and drink properly). Spells like Greater Restoration remove a level instantly. The new scale (−2 per level) fully replaces the discrete effects from 2014.

Calendar.Intro: A year in this homebrew calendar has 365 days. It consists of 12 months of 30 days each, divided into 3 ten-day weeks. Between the months sit 5 special holidays that do not count as month days. Every 4 years adds a sixth leap-year holiday.

Holiday.NewYearDesc: The first holiday of the year, before the 1st month.
Holiday.SpringDesc: Holiday after the 3rd month — start of the warm season.
Holiday.MidsummerDesc: Holiday after the 6th month — middle of the year.
Holiday.HarvestDesc: Holiday after the 9th month — end of the harvest.
Holiday.WinterDesc: Holiday after the 12th month — shortest day of the year.
Holiday.LeapDesc: Additional leap-year holiday placed right after Midsummer, every 4 years.
